analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA new power to prevent, detect, and order recalls of contaminated food.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 298-119 in 2009, cleared the Senate by voice vote in December 2010, and was signed into law by President Obama on January 4, 2011 (Public Law 111-353).
analysis.plain_summary: This law shifts food safety from reacting to outbreaks to preventing them. Food facilities must analyze hazards and put preventive controls in place; FDA can inspect records, target inspections by risk, order a recall of contaminated food (previously it could only ask), trace products through the supply chain, and make importers verify their foreign suppliers. Small farms and direct-to-consumer sellers like farmers markets are largely exempt, and workers who report food safety violations get whistleblower protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who get food that is less likely to be contaminated and a government that can force a recall instead of negotiating with a company; also honest food producers who no longer compete against corner-cutting rivals, and food workers who report violations and gain legal protection.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA the power to order a food recall directly, instead of asking companies to volunteer.
Requires every covered food facility to identify hazards and put preventive controls in place, and establishes science-based standards for growing and harvesting produce.
Requires FDA to target inspections by known risk, build a system to trace contaminated food through the supply chain, and expand foodborne-illness surveillance.
Requires importers to verify that foreign suppliers meet U.S. safety standards, and lets FDA refuse food outright if a foreign facility refuses inspection.
Protects food-industry employees who report safety violations from retaliation.
Exempts small farms and producers selling directly to consumers — roadside stands, farmers markets, CSAs — from the major new requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, processors, and importers, who bear the cost of preventive controls, higher inspection fees for failures, recall-related fees, and supplier verification; some of that may be passed to shoppers as slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs — hazard analyses, preventive controls, produce standards, and fees for failed reinspections and botched recalls — fall on food companies, and small producers argued they could be pushed toward consolidation because larger firms absorb regulatory costs more easily.

The bill relies on FDA rulemaking to fill in the details, and it authorizes appropriations rather than fully funding the added inspections, so the actual strength of enforcement depended on later budget decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefits — mandatory recall authority, prevention-based safety planning, risk-based inspections, tighter import verification, and legal protection for whistleblowers — address real, documented harms like deadly E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks. The costs fall on food producers as compliance burdens and on consumers to the extent companies pass them on, though the bill exempts or phases in smaller operations to soften that. Critics' worry that rules written for big factories would squeeze small farms was partly answered with exemptions, but not eliminated. On balance the public-health gain is large and the cost is a modest, targeted regulatory burden on industry.

outcome.mechanism: After a more than year-long gap between House and Senate action, the Senate attached its food safety language to this already-passed House bill in a December 2010 amendment, the House agreed to that amendment 215-144, and the President signed it on January 4, 2011.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 298-119 on June 9, 2009, under a rule suspension procedure that requires a two-thirds majority; 239 of 256 voting Democrats and 59 of 178 Republicans voted yes.
The bill then sat on the Senate calendar for about eighteen months with no action.

In December 2010, the Senate passed its own food safety legislation, but a technical problem with that bill's revenue provisions made it unusable as-is, so the Senate amendment text was attached to this House bill and passed by voice vote on December 19, 2010.
The House agreed to the Senate amendments 215-144 on December 21, 2010 — 205 of 254 voting Democrats yes, only 10 of 179 Republicans yes.
President Obama signed it into law on January 4, 2011 as Public Law 111-353.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers gained stronger food safety protections; food companies took on new compliance costs but lost the discretion to handle contamination without government-ordered recalls.

sides.party_line_note: The first House vote was broad and bipartisan (298-119, with 59 of 178 Republicans yes), but the final House vote on the Senate amendments split sharply by party: 205 of 254 Democrats yes versus only 10 of 179 Republicans.

industries.note: They must build hazard-analysis and preventive-control programs, open records to FDA, and pay fees when reinspections or government-managed recalls become necessary. The bill's fees and recall authority are aimed precisely at shifting some safety costs from the public onto producers.

Subject to new science-based produce safety standards, but small farms selling mostly directly to consumers under $500,000 a year are exempt, and compliance timelines are stretched for smaller operations.

Importers take on supplier-verification duties and fees, but the bill also creates a voluntary qualified importer program for faster review and a formal system accrediting third-party auditors, which gives auditing firms a sanctioned role in food safety certification.

industries.industry: Food retailers and consumers as payers
industries.note: To the extent compliance costs are passed through, grocery prices carry some of the burden — the tradeoff weighed against fewer outbreaks, recalls, and deaths.
